t: Romanticism was a movement in literature, art, music and thought that from the 1790s prized feeling, imagination and nature over the rules and reason that had governed the arts of the 18th century.
Its poets, painters and composers, from Wordsworth and Byron to Victor Hugo, Caspar David Friedrich and Chopin, celebrated the individual, wild landscape, the Middle Ages and folk traditions.
It gave Europe’s nations poets, epics and fairy-tale collections and fed both liberal revolt and conservative nostalgia, until Realism displaced it around the middle of the 19th century.
dyk: The cold, wet summer of 1816, which followed the eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia, kept Lord Byron and his guests indoors at the Villa Diodati by Lake Geneva, where his ghost-story contest led Mary Shelley to write Frankenstein.
ev: William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge publish Lyrical Ballads; the Schlegel brothers found the Athenaeum
The Brothers Grimm publish the first volume of their Children’s and Household Tales
A ghost-story contest by Lake Geneva starts Mary Shelley on Frankenstein, published in 1818
Adam Mickiewicz’s Ballads and Romances open the Romantic age of Polish literature
Lord Byron dies at Missolonghi while aiding the Greek War of Independence
Victor Hugo’s Hernani causes uproar in Paris; Hector Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique is first performed
Elias Lönnrot publishes the Kalevala, the epic of Finland, from songs collected in Karelia
Revolutions sweep Europe; the poets Alphonse de Lamartine and Sándor Petőfi stand among their leaders

f.where: Arose in Germany and Britain in the 1790s; spread to France, Italy, Spain, Poland, Russia, Scandinavia and the Americas
f.period: c. 1790–1850: from the Jena circle and Lyrical Ballads of 1798 to the revolutions of 1848; forerunners in the Sturm und Drang of the 1770s, and echoes in music to the end of the 19th century
f.figures: Friedrich Schlegel, William Wordsworth, Lord Byron, Victor Hugo, Caspar David Friedrich, Frédéric Chopin
f.outcome: Changed literature, painting and music for good, made feeling and imagination central to art, and fed nationalism and the study of folklore and history; gave way to Realism after about 1850
